Anemia: Decreased red cell mass leading to decreased oxygen carrying capacity of body.

Morphological classification

1-Normocytic Normochromic anemia: A decrease in hemoglobin, PCV and RBCs count with normal MCV, MCH and MCHC. The most common causes are: a)Hemolytic anemia b)Post-hemorrhagic anemia in acute blood loss. c)Anemia of chronic disorder b)Aplastic anemia. c)Bone marrow infiltration d)Myelodysplastic syndrome e)Congenital dyserythropoietic anemia 2-Microcytic Hypochromic anemia: A decrease in hemoglobin, PCV and may be RBCs count with low MCV, MCH and MCHC. The most common causes are: a)Iron deficiency. b)Thalassemia. c)Sideroblastic anemia. d)Some unstable hemoglobinopathies e)HbC and HbE. f)Congenital atransferrinemia g)Anemia of chronic disorders h)Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria 3-Macrocytic anemia: A decrease in hemoglobin, PCV and RBCs count with High MCV. The most common causes are: i-Megaloblastic anemia (associated with pancytopenia) a)Vitamin B12 or folate deficiency b)Congenital dyserythropoietic anemia 4

Original page 5

ii-Normoblastic (non megaloblastic, no pancytopenia):

a)Pregnancy and newborns due to the high steroid level b)Chronic respiratory failure c)Alcoholism d)Liver disease and obstructive jaundice e)Hypothyroidism f)Aplastic anemia g)Myelodysplasia h)Myeloma i)Reticulocytosis j)Leucoerythroblastic reaction k)Postsplenectomy because spleen removes a part of the red cell membrane

Etiological classification

1-Deficiency of building materials:

a)Iron deficiency anemia b)Megaloblastic anemia: Vitamin B12 and folate deficiency c)Protein Caloric malnutrition 2-Bone marrow disease: a)Aplastic anemia b)BM infiltration by leukemia, lymphoma, multiple myeloma, fibrosis or granuloma 3-Blood loss: a)Acute blood loss: Normocytic or macrocytic anemia due to reticulocytosis b)Chronic blood loss: Microcytic hypochromic anemia due to iron deficiency 4-Hemolytic anemia 5-Dilutional anemia as in pregnancy or splenomegaly. 5

Original page 6

Hypoproliferative Anemia: Anemia with BM erythropoiesis and reticulocytic count lower than what is expected for the degree of anemia. It may be caused by: 1- Low erythropoietin

○Chronic renal failure.

○Endocrine disease.

○Protein caloric malnutrition.

○Low hemoglobin oxygen affinity.

○Inflammation.

2-Shortage in iron absolute deficiency in iron deficiency anemia or functional deficiency as

anemia of chronic disorders.

3-Damage of the bone marrow:

○Chemotherapy.

○Radiotherapy.

○Infiltration.

Causes of Reticulocytopenia:

1- Aplastic anemia. 2- Ineffective erythropoiesis. 3. Myelodysplastic syndrome. 4. Aplastic crisis in hemolytic anemia. 5. Leukemia (variable). Bone marrow depression by drugs, chemotherapy, irradiation or infection.

Causes of Reticulocytosis

1-Hyperactive erythropoiesis as in hemorrhage, hemolysis, hematinic intake or hypersplenism. b)Polycythemia. c)Bone marrow infiltration by multiple mieloma, lymphoma, leukemia, metastatic carcinoma, myelofibrosis, marble bone disease, storage diseases (Niemman Pick and Gaucher). d)Post-splenectomy. 6

Normoblastemia: Presence of nucleated red blood precursors in the peripheral blood. It may be caused by: 1.Hemorrhage: There will be a history of blood loss accompanied by normocytic normochromic anemia and reticulocytosis. 2.Hemolytic anemias and hemolytic crisis: There will be a normocytic normochromic anemia, reticulocytosis, jaundice and increased serum indirect bilirubin and low serum haptoglobin. 3.Post-splenectomy: There will be a history of splenectomy, transient neutrophilia and thrombocytosis, permenant lymphocytosis and monocytosis, reticulocytosis and red blood corpuscles anisopoikilocytosis. 4.Thalassemia: There will be a positive family history, splenomegaly, history of splenectomy, history of blood transfusion, microcytic hypochromic anemia, slightly elevated reticulocytic count, elevated serum indirect bilirubin and evidence of thalassemia in hemogl;obin electrophoresis, HPLC and genetic tests. 5.Bone marrow infiltration: There will be a leukoerythroblastic anemia and bone marrow evidence of infiltration with either: - Multiple mieloma. - Lymphoma. - Leukemia. - Metastatic carcinoma. - Myelofibrosis. - Storage diseases (Niemman Pick and Gaucher). 7

Iron and Heme Metabolism

Iron Metabolism

•Definition of iron metabolism: It is the set of chemical reactions maintaining homeostasis of iron at both the systemic and cellular level.

•Distribution of body iron: Total body iron is 3-5 gm. (♂ 50 mg/kg, ♀ 40 mg/kg). Essential iron in the form of myoglobin and enzymes is not available for erythropoiesis.

Function of iron

1-Hb: For gas transport 2- Enzymes:

–Cyclooxygenase: Prostaglandin synthesis.

–Cytochromes oxidase (a, b, c) and succinate dehydrogenase: electron transport.

–Cytochrome P450: hydroxylation reactions

–Catalase and lactoperoxidase: peroxide breakdown.

–Tryptophan pyrrolase: oxidation of tryptophan.

–Ribonucleotide reductase: a key enzyme for DNA synthesis.

–Iron sulphur proteins: xanthine oxidase, reduced nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide dehydrogenase and aconitase. 3- Integrity of epithelial cells. 4- Myoglobin: Local tissue reservoir of O2, facilitates intracellular O2 diffusion in muscles and scavenges free radicals. 5- Mitochondria: citric acid cycle. 6-Nervous tissues: Development, Synaptic activity and Myelination. 7- Immunity: T cell number and function and myeloperoxidase in macrophages:. 8

Original page 9

Iron intake

○Dietary sources: Iron is high in liver, kidney, heart, muscle, brewer’s yeast, wheat germ, egg yolks, oysters, some dried beans and some fruits, intermediate in green vegetables, cereals, fish and fowl and low in milk, milk products and most non-green vegetables.

○Daily requirement: 10-20 mg, 5-10 mg is soluble after digestion, 3 mg are taken by intestinal cells, 1-2 mg are transferred to circulation (5-10% of intake).

•Iron absorption: In the duodenum and upper jejunum: +++++ I-Non-heme iron: Fe is reduced to Fe by the action of Duodenal cytochrome b ++ reductase at the brush border of the duodenal cells → Feenters duodenal cells through ++ the Divalent metal transporter 1 at the brush border of the duodenal cells→ Feis transferred across the duodenal mucosa where it is either stored as ferritin or exported ++ +++ through the Ferroportin → Feis oxidized into Fe by the action of Haephasatin at the +++ basal border of the duodenal cells → Fe is carried on Transferrin II-Heme iron: Heme enters duodenal cells through the Heme carrier protein 1 at the brush border of the duodenal cells → Hemeis then transferred across the duodenal mucosa where ++ it is either digested by the action of Heme Oxygenase into Feor exported as it is through the Feline leukemia virus group C receptor at the basal border of the duodenal cells where it is carried on the Hemopexin to the liver.

Factors affecting iron absorption:

I-Dietary factors:

1-Heme iron is more absorbable 2-Iron in animal food is more absorbable because of the irect availability of heme iron and unidentified ligand in meat that increases the availability of non-haem iron. +++++ 3-Fe is more absorbable than Fe. 4-Sugars and amino acids facilitate iron absorption because they facilitate attachment of iron to duodenum, while tannins, phosphates, phytates, and oxalates form insoluble salts with iron decreasing its absorption. 9

Original page 10

II-Luminal factors: Absorption of heme iron is not affected by luminal factors:

1-Acid pH and vitamin C prevents iron precipitation as insoluble ferric hydroxide whereas alkaline pH (as in gastectomy and achlorhydria) precipitates iron as insoluble ferric hydroxide 2-Therapeutic ferrous ion salts are well absorbed on an empty stomach due to some ligand-binding processes III-Systemic factors: 1-Absorption of iron increases with ion deficiency (↑ Absorption down to 30%), anemia, hypoxia, increased erythropoiesis, ineffective erythropoiesis, erythropoietin utilization and primary hemochromatosis 2-Absorption of iron ↓ with: ↑ iron stores (↓ Absorption to 2-5%) and inflammation.

•Iron Transport (Transferrin): One molecule of transferrin binds 2 atoms of ferric iron and transports iron (>30 mg/day) from gastrointestinal tract, reticulo-endothelial system and liver parenchyma to cells with transferrin receptors. 1-Transferrin receptors1 = CD71:

○Structure: It has 2 forms: Trans-membrane form and truncated soluble form.

○Distribution: Normoblasts (maximum on intermediate normoblasts) and rapidly dividing cells as gastrointestinal tract, genital tract and placenta.

○Function: Entrance of the holotransferrin and transferrin receptor 1 inside the cells through a receptor mediated endocytosis → lowering of the pH of the by the action +++ of proton pump → dissociation of Fe from the holotransferrin and its reduction into ++++ Fe → Fe is then either stored as ferritin or used in heme synthesis → Recycling of transferrin and transferrin receptor to the cell surface → re-use of the receptor and circulation of the Transferrin in the plasma

○Regulation of synthesis: Iron and erythropoietic activity 2-Transferrin receptors2: Regulates iron homeostasis by regulating hepcidin synthesis in response to holotransferrin. 10

Iron Balance

–Daily iron intake (1-2 mg) = daily iron loss (1-2mg) with most of iron required for erythropoiesis is derived from RBCs recycling.

–Regulation of cellular iron: Iron regulatory protein (IRP) and Iron responsive elements (IREs).

–Regulation of systemic iron: hepcidin. Intracellular iron: It is divided into three pools: 1-Transient pool (labile pool): in exchange with the circulating transferrin. 2-Storage pool (cytosolic ferritin): can be mobilized when required. 3-Functional pool (for synthesis of heme and iron sulfur proteins): extra-mitochondrial and mitochondrial. 12

Original page 13

Cellular iron Homeostasis (translational): IRP1 and IRP2 are capable of binding to IRE which is a stem and loop structure in the mRNA in proteins involved in iron metabolism.

➢IRP1: When cellular iron is high, it acts as aconitase and can’t bind to IRE while when cellular iron is low, It binds to IRE

➢IRP2: When cellular iron is high, It is degraded and can’t bind to IRE while when cellular iron is low, It binds to IRE

➢IRE of Transferrin receptor 1 – Divalent transporter 1 – Ferroportin is at 3 of mRNA and / binding of IRP to IRE in these proteins stabilizes mRNA and increases translation.

➢IRE of ferritin and Amino-leveulinic acid synthase enzyme (involved in heme synthesis) is at 5 of mRNA and binding of IRP to IRE in these proteins blocks translation. /

Systemic Iron homeostasis (Hepcidin):

➢Gene: HAMP gene on chromosome 19.

➢Site of synthesis: Mainly in the liver but may be synthesized in macrophages, adipose tissues, heart, placenta and kidney, where it is regulated by inflammatory cytokines rather than iron.

➢Action: It decreases iron export from macrophages, hepatocytes and gastrointestinal cells. It acts on ferroportin causing its JAK2 mediated tyrosine phosphorylation, internalization, ubiquitination and degradation in lysosomes.

➢Regulation: 1-Factors increasing Hepcidin: Increased iron stores and inflammation 2-Factors decreasing Hepcidin: Iron deficiency, anemia, hypoxia, increased erythropoiesis, ineffective erythropoiesis, erythropoietin utilization and primary hemochromatosis 13

1-Investigations of iron stores:

–Serum Ferritin

3-Investigations of functioning iron:

–Hb concentration

–MCV and MCH Serum Ferritin: (N:15-300 μg/L in males, 15-200 μg/L in premenopausal female)

•Clinical uses: It correlates with tissue iron stores.

Causes of high serum Ferritin

Increased body iron stores e.g.: primary hemochromatosis or hemolytic anemia. Acute phase e.g.: inflammation, infection or malignancy. Non utilization of iron e.g.: aplastic and megaloblastic anemia. Organ damage e.g.: hepatic necrosis or splenic infarction. Hereditary hyperferritinaemia with autosomal dominant cataract syndrome.

•Causes of low Serum Ferritin: Low body iron stores in iron deficiency anemia. 14

Liver biopsy:

•Liver iron overload means that liver iron is > 80μmol/g dry weight (>4.5 mg/g dry weight).

•Hepatic iron index: iron (μmol) /g dry weight/age in years (> 2.0 means iron overload). N.B.: Other methods for assessment of liver iron: 1-MRI: non invasive. 2-superconducting quantum interface device (SQUID): expensive

Bone marrow biopsy with iron Stain (Perl’s Test or Prussian Blue Test)

•Principle: Potassium ferrocyanide (iron stain) + Hemosiderin → Ferriferrocyanide (blue). N.B.: By Leishman’s stain, hemosiderin granules are stained as peripheralbasophilic inclusions called Pappenheimer bodies which may be single or in pairs. I.Normal conditions: Siderocyte areabsent in peripheral blood because they are removed from reticulocytes in the spleen. BM. Sideroblast (30-40% of normoblasts) contains one or few granules difficult to be seen and randomly distributed in the cytoplasm. II.Iron deficiency: ↓ sideroblasts and ↓ siderotic granules in normoblasts and macrophages. III.Anemia of chronic disorders: ↓ Siderotic granules in normoblasts and ↑ siderotic granules in macrophages. IV.Iron overload: ↑ sideroblasts. ↑ Siderotic granules in normoblasts and macrophages, easily visible and randomly distributed V.Sideroblastic anemia: iron precipitates between the cristae of mitochondria located around the nucleus. Ringed sideroblasts are sideroblasts in which there are at least 6 granules around the nucleus or granules are surrounding 1\3 of the nucleus. N.B.: Ringed sideroblasts are found in the following conditions:

○Sideroblastic anemia

○Idiopathic myelofibrosis.

○Acute myeloblastic leukemia particularly M6.

○Therapy related acute myeloblastic leukemia

○Acute myeloblastic leukemia with multilineage dysplasia. Chelation test: IM 0.5g desferroxamine →24 hour urinary iron (N: 2mg/day). 15

Phelopotomy test: 25 Weekly venesection of 450 ml blood with allowingabsorption of 3 mg iron daily → Calculation of iron removed till iron depletion(N: 450 mL blood with Hb 13.5 g/dL contains 200 mg of iron). Serum Iron: (N: 60 – 170 μg/dL)

Disadvantages

A-Non-specific for iron deficiency: Low in anemia of chronic disorders. B-Labile; varing from day to day, more in morning and more in children.

•Causes of high Serum Iron: Primary or Secondary Hemochromatosisi e.g.: Hemolytic anemias, ineffective erythropoiesis, aplastic anemia, parenteral iron therapy and repeated blood transfusion.

Causes of low Serum Iron

Iron deficiency anemia. Anemia of chronic disorders. Congenital atransferrinaemia. Nephrotic syndrome due to the loss of transferrin in urine. Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria due to the loss of transferrin in urine. Serum TIBC: (N: 250 – 400 μg/dL)

Disadvantages

▪Non-specific for iron deficiency: Low in anemia of chronic disorders.

▪Labile; varing from day to day, more in morning and more in children.

•Causes of high TIBC: Iron deficiency anemia

•Causes of low TIBC: Primary or Secondary Hemochromatosisi e.g.: Hemolytic anemias, ineffective erythropoiesis, aplastic anemia, parenteral iron therapy and repeated blood transfusion. Anemia of chronic disorder. Congenital atransferrinemia. Nephrotic syndrome. 16

Transferrin saturation: It is the earliest parameter to be changed in iron overload (N: 15 – 50%). Levels less than 15% is insufficient to support erythropoiesis.

Soluble transferrin receptor:

–Differentiation between early iron deficiency anemia (↑) and anemia of chronic disorders Soluble transferrin receptors (↓) but ratios has a higher sensitivity and specificity. Log of serum ferritin

–In absence of iron deficiency anemia, it is a good indicator for erythropoiesis. Red cell protoporphyrin: More than 80 umol/ml Hb in iron deficiency anemia

Red cell ferritin

Percentage ofHypochromic red cells: More than 6% in iron deficiency anemia Reticulocyte Hb content: Less than 32 pg in iron deficiency anemia

Uses of the last four tests

1-Early diagnosis of iron deficiency anemia 2-Differential diagnosis of:

–Iron deficiency anemia from anemia of chronic disorders.

–Iron deficiency anemia from thalassemia minor.

Disadvantages

1-They assess iron at the time of red cell production but not the current status. 2-Non-specific: They are ffected by any factor interfering with iron incorporation in red cells as sideroblastic anemia, lead poisoning and inflammation. 17

Iron Deficiency Anemia

The most common anemia Definition: Decreases in Hb concentration of hemoglobin due to lack of iron.

Causes:

1-Chronic Blood Loss of at least 6-8 ml/day (the commonest): Menstrual, pregnancy or labor related, GIT, Hemoptysis, epistaxis, hematuria and hemoglobinuria. 2-Increased requirements: Infancy especially prematurity, adolescence, pregnancy or lactation. 3-Decreased iron absorption: Malabsorption, gasterectomy and achlorohydria. 4-Decreased dietary iron intake: in starvation. Anorexia, malnutrition and vegetarians

Stages and Pathogenesis:

1.Depletion of iron stores (prelatent stage):  Hemosiderin in macrophages and  ferritin. 2.Iron deficiency (iron deficient erythropoiesis / latent stage): The above +  Serum iron, TIBC,  Transferrin saturation to less than 15%, soluble transferrin receptor  Red cell protoporphyrin and ↓ MCV and MCH. 3.Iron deficiency anemia: The above +  Hemoglobin and  PCV,  Transferrin saturation to less than 10%,  Sideroblast and ↓ siderotic granules in normoblasts. 4.Ineffective erythropoiesis: The above + intramedullary hemolysis and  RBCs life span with↑ indirect bilirubin, urobilinogen and sterchobilin and decreased Haptoglobin. 5.Tissue effects of iron deficiency:The above +  Iron containing enzymesleading to: a-Koilonychia, angular stomatitis, glossitis, atrophic gastritis, pharyngeal web, Plummer Vinson Syndrome, Paterson-Kelly syndrome (angular stomatitis, glossitis, pharyngeal webs and flat brittle nail Kolionychia), dysphagia and pica b-Impaired cell mediated immunity and phagocytosis c-Impaired work performance. d-Infants: impaired mental development (not completely reversible) and partial villous atrophy e-Pregnancy: premature labor. 18

Clinical Picture

–Dizziness, weakness, tiredness and blurring of vision.

–Clinical picture of the cause

–Clinical picture of tissue iron deficiency (if severe and chronic): Tissue changes.

Laboratory Diagnosis:

–CBC:  Hb,  RBCs,  PCV,  MCV,  MCH,  MCHC, ↑RDW, normal TLC with Eosinophilia in parasitic infestations and thrombocytosis.

–Blood film: microcytic hypochromic RBCs, anisocytosis, poikilocytosis, ovalocytosis, target cells and elliptocytes.

–Bone Marrow: Hypercellular with erythroid hyperplasia and  or reversed M/E ratio. The predominant cells are late normoblasts which are smaller with delayed hemoglobinization and ragged cytoplasm. Perl’ s stain shows  sideroblast and  siderotic granules in normoblasts and macrophages.

–Investigations to detect the cause: Occult blood in stool, stool analysis. GIT endoscopy and radiography as barium enema and meal, Chest X-ray, Urine analysis and Pelvic examination in women. N.B.: The earliest changes are:  RDW,  Ferritin,  erythrocyte free protoporphyrin,  soluble transferrin receptor and  percentage of hypochromic red cells. IRON OVERLOAD (Hemochromatosis)

•Definition: Abnormal accumulation of iron in parenchymal organs, leading to organ toxicity.

Causes

–Hereditary Hemochromarosis.

–Ineffective erythropoiesis: Thalassemia major and intermedia, congenital dyserythropoietic anemia and sideroblastic anemia.

– Increased iron intake: African (Sub-Saharan) dietary iron overload, excess parenteral iron therapy and chronic Ingestion of oral iron tablets.

–Repeated red cell transfusions.

–Modest iron overload (<5g excess): Chronic liver disease, Porphyria cutanea tarda, congenial Atransferrinemia and congenital Aceruloplasminemia.

–Focal iron overload: Pulmonary hemorrhage, idiopathic pulmonary hemosiderosis, Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, Friedreich’s ataxia (mitochondrial) and hereditary hyperferritinemia with autosomal dominant congenital cataract.

•Pathogenesis: 1-Peroxidation of the lipids of the cell membranes. 2-Oxidation of intracellular proteins. 3-Damage of the lysosomal membrane and release of lysosomal enzymes.

Hereditary (Genetic) Hemochromatosis (HH)

21

Original page 22

Type 1 Hemochromatosis (The most common): Autosomal recessive mutation of HFE gene on chromosome 6 close to HLA-A locus →↓ hepcidin → ↓ its inhibitory effect on ferroportin1 → ↑ iron egress from macrophages, hepatocytes and deudenal cells → ↑ Plasma iron level → ↑ iron deposition in parynchemal organs → tissue damage →

–Arrhythmias, cardiomyopathy and congestive heart failure.

–Hepatosplenomegaly; cirrhosis, portal hypertension, liver cell failure and hepatoma (25%).

–Diabetes milletus, hypothyroidism, hypoadrenalism and hypogonadism.

–Grey pigmentation due to the increased melanin deposition in (Bronze diabetes).

–Arthritis particularly of hand joints and chondrocalcinosis. The most common mutations are: a-C282Y: tyrosine substitution for cysteine at amino acid 282 b-H63D: aspartate substitution for histidine at amino acid 63 N.B.: Function of HFE protein: Regulation of iron homeostasis through:

–↑ Hepcidin

–↓ Affinity of transferrin receptors to Transferrin.

–↓ Iron egress and transferrin recycling from transferrin cycle endosome. Type 2 (Juvenile) Hemochromatosis (Rare): Autosomal recessivemutation of Hemojuvenile gene on chromosome (1) or HAMP gene on chromosome (19)→↓ hepcidin → ↓ its inhibitory effect on ferroportin → ↑ iron egress from macrophages, hepatocytes and deudenal cells → ↑ Plasma iron level → ↑ iron deposition in parynchemal organs → tissue damage→ Severe ndrd presentation with cardiomyopathy and hypogonadism in 2 or 3 decaded of life. Type 3 Hemochromatosis (Rare): Autosomal recessive mutation of Transferrin receptor2 gene on chromosome (3) →↓ hepcidin → ↓ its inhibitory effect on ferroportin → ↑ iron egress from macrophages, hepatocytes and deudenal cells → ↑ Plasma iron level → ↑ iron deposition in parynchemal organs → tissue damage → presentation similar to type 1 but more severe. 22

Original page 23

Type 4 Hemochromatosis (Rare):Autosomal dominant mutation of Ferroportin gene on chromosome (2) leading to either:

–↓ Ferroprtin (More common) → ↓ iron egress from macrophages, hepatocytes and deudenal cells → ↑ iron deposition in reticuloendothelial organs → less tissue damage

–↓ Ferroprtin degradation by hepcidin (less common) → ↑ iron egress from macrophages, hepatocytes and deudenal cells → ↑ iron deposition in parynchemal organs → tissue damage with ↑ Serum ferritin, normal Transferrin saturation and ↑iron in both parenchymal and reticuloendothelial cells.

Other causes of Congenital iron overload

–Nenatal iron overload: Immunogenic and treated by IV Ig and hepatic transplantation

–Increased iron intake: Sub-Saharan (African) dietary iron overload (Bantu siderosis) due to consumption of traditional beer + ferroportin mutation + alcoholism + malnutration + infection → ↑ Serum ferritin, normal Transferrin saturation and ↑ Iron in both parenchymal and reticuloendothelial cells.

–Congenital Atransferrinemia: Autosomal recessive mutation decreasing the Transferrin (Complete absence is fetal) → Sever microcytic hypochromic anemia,  Serum iron,  TIBC,  Serum ferritin and  Iron deposition in tissues.

–Aceruloplasminemia: Autosomal recessive Rare mutation of ceruloplasmin gene on chromosome (3) → Ceruloplasmin ferroxidase activity → Iron accumulation in liver, pancreas, CNS, heart, kidney, spleen, retina and thyroid → progressive neurodegeneration of retina and basal ganglia and DM in the middle age with  Serum iron, Normal TIBC and Normal or  Serum ferritin.

–Friedreich s ataxia: Autosomal recessive mutation of friedrich’ s gene on chromosome (9)  Frataxin which regulates mitochondrial iron → iron accumulation in mitochondria  oxidative damage  Spinocerebellar degeneration cardiomyopathy and at middle age.

–Hereditary hyperferritinemia with autosomal dominant congenital cataract: Autosomal dominant mutation of the iron responsive element loop of mRNA of L- ferritin → synthesis of ferritin L chain  deposition in lens (cataract) and other organs.

–Neuroferritinopathy: Autosomal dominant mutation in the gene coding for ferritin L chain → ↑ ferritin and iron in the forebrain and cerebellum (extrapyramidal dysfunction) with low serum ferritin.

–Hallervorden-Spatz syndrome: Autosomal recessive mutation of pantothenate kinase → ↑ Cysteine with its binding iron → oxidative stess in the basal ganglia → extrapyramidal dysfunction. 23

Original page 24

Laboratory Diagnosis

–Transferrin saturation: > 55% in males and 50% in females. It is the earliest to be changed and the most sensitive test.

– Serum iron,  Serum ferritin and TIBC.

–Liver biopsy: liver iron is more than 80μmol/g dry weight (4.5 mg/g dry weight)

–Bone marrow iron stain: ↑ sideroblasts. Siderotic granules are numerous, increased in both normoblasts and macrophages, directly proportional with transferrin saturation, easily visible and randomly distributed

–Skin biopsy iron deposition in the skin.

–Chelation test: 24 hour urinary iron in is > 2 mg after IM of 0.5g desferroxamine

–Phlebotomy test: More iron removed through weekly venesections till iron depletion.

–Ferrokinetics: very little iron is incorporated in red cells.

–B-Monitoring of iron induced tissue damage organ: ECG ,Echo, MRI,  aminotransferases,blood glucose, HbA1c, urine glucose T4,  T3 , TSH, growth hormone, FSH, LH andbone density.

–Genotyping by PCR: definitive diagnosis.

–Family testing: Transferrin saturation, serum ferritin and genotyping.

•Treatment: Regular phlebotomy to get transferrin saturation < 50% and serum ferritin less than 50µg/L with iron chelator: desferrioxamine, deferiprone or ICL670. 24

Original page 25

Sideroblastic Anemia

Definition: Refractory anemias due to blockage of heme synthesis due to protoporphyrin defect.

Causes and classification:

Hereditary Sideroblastic Anemia (rare): > 25 X linked missense or point mutation of the erythroid specific amino-leveulinic acid synthase 2 either in the Pyridine binding site, the catalytic active site or in the promotor. 25

Original page 26

ABCB7 mutations: Mutations in the ATP binding cassette transporter gene that blocks the maturation of iron sulphur clusters. Pearson syndrome: Pancytopenia: macrocytosis, sideroblastic anemia, prominent vacuoles in both myeloid and erythroid lineages, liver and renal dysfunction and exocrine pancreatic dysfunction with persistent diarrhea, failure to thrive and lactic acidosis. Kearns-Sayre syndrome: Renal and visual impairment (retinitis pigmentosa), muscle weakness and ataxia. Pathogenesis: Intramitochondrial defects in heme synthesis leads to mitochondrial iron loading and mitochondrial damage which aggravates the heme synthesis defect N.B.: Sex linked diseases include 1-Haemophilia A & B 2-G6PD deficiency 3-Sideroblastic anemia 4-Wiskott Aldrich Syndrome Clinical picture: Hereditary cases are presented in the first few weeks or months of life, in childhood or adolescence. Late presentation occurs occasionally. It occurs mainly in male but female carriers may show partial or severe affection according to the degree of lyonization of the affected X chromosome. Manifestations include pallor, hepatosplenomegaly, frontal bossing and spinocerebellar ataxia.

Laboratory Diagnosis:

Lead Poisoning

•Definition: It is a type of metal poisoning caused by accumulation of lead in the body

Causes and Persons at high risk of exposure are

•Painters in old buildings.

•Battery factory workers.

•Children ingesting flakes of lead

Pathogenesis

–Inhibition of mitochondrial enzymes of haem synthesis especially amino-leveulinic acid synthase 2 and ferrochelatase leading to sideroblastic anemia.

–Inhibition of globin synthesis

–Hemolytic anemia: block of sulfhyryl group leading to denaturation of structural proteins of RBCs membrane.

–Inhibition of pyrimidine 5`-nucleotidase decreases the breakdown of RNA leading to accumulation of RNA which results in the basophilic stippling.

•Clinical picture: Asymptomatic or nonspecific symptoms as headache, abdominal pain, renal failure, tingling, insomnia, delirium, cognitive deficit, tremors, hallucination and convulsions.

Laboratory Diagnosis

–Blood film: Basophilic stippling, siderotic granules, Cabot ring and normoblastemia.

–Reticulocytosis

–Bone marrow: Erythroid hyperplasia with ↑ sideroblast and sometimes ring sideroblasts.

Disorders of vitamin B12 and Folate Metabolism

Vitamin B12 (Cobalamin) Metabolism

Structure:Corrin ring of porphyrin structure with a cobalt atom in the center, nucleotide and - group which is either methyl, adenosyl, cyano, or hydroxyl group:

–5'Deoxyadenosyl cobalamin: in mitochondria acting as a cofactor for methylmalonyl CoA mutase enzyme.

–Methyl cobalamin: in plasma and cytoplasm acting as a cofactor for methionine synthase enzyme.

–Hydroxocobalamin to which 5'deoxyadenosyl and methyl cobalamin are rapidly converted by exposure to light. Dietary sources and requirements: Animal food only as liver, kidney, meat, fish, egg, chicken and milk.Daily requirement is 1-2 g and 2-3 mg are stored in liver and are sufficient for 3-4 yrs. Absorption: Absorption occurs by both active and passive processes: A-Active Mechanism: 𝐺𝑎𝑠𝑡𝑟𝑜𝑖𝑛𝑡𝑒𝑠𝑡𝑖𝑛𝑎𝑙 𝑒𝑛𝑧𝑦𝑚𝑒𝑠

○The fate of the intrinsic factor is unkowm

○Cobalmin appears after 6 hours in the portal circulation carried on transcobalamin II that undergoes enterohepatic circulation where it is secreted in bile binding to R-binder and the cycle is repeated.0.5-9g vitamin B12 circulate in the enterohepatic circulation per day B-Passive mechanism: 10% of dietary vitamin B12 are absorbed by a passive process which doesn’t require the intrinsic factor from the duodenum, ilium, sublingual and nasal epithelium. 31

Transport and Uptake

1-Transcobalamin II (TCII) = TC

○Synthesis: endothelial cells - ileum - liver.

○Function: carriage of vitamin B12 from intestine to the target tissues (liver for storage or bone marrow for erythropoiesis) within minutes after appearance in blood. 10-30% of plasma vitamin B12 is carried on TCII. It is largely unsaturated with vitamin B12.

○Receptors: in many types of tissues. Megalin receptors are specific receptors in the kidney to prevent its loss in urine. Binding to receptors is followed by a receptor mediated pinocytosis, where TC II is digested and Cobalamin becomes free.

○Half-life: one hour.

○Causes of high level of plasma TCII: liver diseases, Gucher’s disease, autimmune disease and Hydroxycobalamin therapy.

2-Transcobalamin I(TC I) (HC) (R binder):

○Site: gastric juice, saliva, bile, milk and other body fluids.

○Synthesis: granulocytes.

○Function: functionally dead as it has no receptors on tissues. It transports cobalamin analogues to the liver for excretion. 70-90% of plasma vitamin B12 are carried on TCI. >2/3 of it are saturated with vitamin B12

○Half-life: 10 days.

○Causes of high level of plasma TCI: MPN and other causes of increased granulocytic production, hepatoma and hypereosinophilic syndrome. 3-Transcobalamin III (TCIII): isoprotein of TCI in plasma synthesized in leucocytes differs from it by its composition of sugars and cobalamin content. 32

○Proteins Maintaining the active form of foloAmines

Congenital methyl malonic aciduria: Vomiting, failure to thrive, ketosis, mental retardation, nomocytic normochromic anemia and neurological defects since birth.

Folate (Vitamin B9) Metabolism

Structure: Pteridine (double ring) + paraaminobenzoic acid + glutamic acid. The active form is Tetra-hydro-folate. Folate monoglutamate traverses membranes more easily while folate polyglutamate: predominates intracellular DietarySources: Green vegetables, nuts, meat, liver and yeast. Cooking in large amount of water the most folic acid content. Daily requirements is 100 ug/day and5-10 mg in the liver which are sufficient only for 4 months. Absorption: Dietary folate exists as folate polyglutamate which has to be hydrolyzed to folate monoglutamate by the action of pteryle polyglutamate hydrolase enzyme at the intestinal brush border to be transported across membranes and enters the cells of the duodenum and upper jejunum through the proton-coupled folate receptor 1 (PCFT1). In the intestinal cells, folate monoglutamate undergoes methylation and reduction to be converted into 5-Methyl tetra-hydro- folate monoglutamate which exits the intestinal cells and enters the circulation after 15-20 minutes Transport: 1/3 of folate is carried on albumin, 2/3 circulate freely and 60-90 gram of folate circulate in the portal circulation daily. Uptake and trapping inside cells: 5-Methyl tetra-hydro-folate monoglutamate is transported into cells by a carrier- or receptor-mediated transport using folate receptor α, folate receptor β, folate receptor γ and reduced folate carrier. → converted into tetra-hydrofolate monoglutamate by tha action of Methionine synthase enzyme and vitamin B12 as a co-factor for the enzyme. In this reaction, homocysteine is converted to methionine which is converted into S adenosyle methionine that is used in the methylation reactions. Tetra-hydro-folate monoglutamate is then converted to tetra-hydro-folate polyglutamate by the action of folate polyglutamate synthase enzyme to be trapped inside the cell. 35

Megaloblastic Anaemia

Definition: Anemia with Megaloblasts in the bone marrow and macrocytes in the peripheral blood due to impairment DNA synthesis resulting from vitamin B12 and/or folate deficiency

Causes

I-Causes of folate deficiency:

1. Dietary:May be associated with scurvy in old age, infancy especially with prematurity, poverty, alcoholism, anorexia nervosa and psychiatric disturbance 2. Malabsorption: Malabsorption syndrome, intestinal megaloblastosis caused by severe cobalamin or folate deficiency and specific malabsorption of folate. 3. Excess utilization or loss:Pregnancy, lactation, prematurity (especially if < 1.5 kg), chronic hemolytic anemia, myelofibrosis, malignancy, inflammation, homocystinuria (due to the compensatory increase in the conversion of homocysteine to methionine with excessive utilization of folate), excess urinary loss in congestive heart failure or active liver disease and chronic hemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis (due to the loss of folate during dialysis). 4. Antifolate drugs: Anticonvulsants, sulphasalazine, methotrexate, trimethoprim, nitrofurantoin, tetracycline or anti-TB drugs. 5. Alcohol:It decreases folate intake, absorption and folate dependent enzymes 5. Congenital abnormalities: Deficiency of cyclohydroxylase or methionine synthetase.

II-Causes of vitamin B12 deficiency:

i-Nutritional:Vegetarians and infants born to severely Cobalamin deficient mother and fed on breast milk of low Cobalamin content. ii-Malabsorption 1-Gastric causes: Congenital intrinsic factor absence or functional abnormality, pernicious anemia, gastrectomy, gastric bypass surgery, proton pump inhibitors, simple atrophic gastritis and Zollinger–Ellison syndrome which inhibits Trypsin decreasing the degradation of R binder. 37

Original page 38

2-Intestinal causes: A.Intestinal stagnant loop syndrome (diverticulosis, ileo-colic fistula, anatomical blind loop and intestinal stricture): Decreased motility leads to intestinal colonization with bacteria which bind Cobalamin. B.Ileal resection (removal of 1.2 m or more of the terminal ileum) and Crohn’s disease: particularly if the ileo-caecal valve is incompetent leading to intestinal colonization C.Tropical sprue: in all patients. D.Gluten-induced enteropathy: in 30% of untreated patients. E.Selective malabsorption with proteinuria (Imerslund–Gräsbeck syndrome): Autosomal recessive impairment of cubilin with normal other tests of intestinal absorption and non-specific proteinuria with normal renal function. F. Fish tapeworm (Diphyllobothrium latum) especially the heavy infestation. G. Severe pancreatitis: Trypsin is required to degrade Cobalamin from the R binder and the low Calcium decreases Cobalamin absorption. I. Radiotherapy: Total body irradiation or local irradiation of the ileum. J. Graft-versus-host disease: The abnormal flora damage the ileal mucosa. 3. Drugs: Colchicine, para-aminosalicylate, neomycin, anticonvulsant drugs, metformin, phenformin, cytotoxic drugs and H2 blockers 4. Alcohol 5.HIV infection: Increases apo-TC because it is derived from macrophages. iii-Abnormalities in Cobalamin metabolism:See before. N.B.: The commonest cause of folate deficiency is nutritional deficiency; whilst the commonest cause of B12 deficiency is the absorption.

III-Other causes::

1.Drugs:Antimetabolites as hydroxyurea, cytosine arabinoside and 6-mercaptopurine. 2.Some cases of Acute myeloid leukemia and Myelodysplastic syndrome 3.Orotic aciduria:defect of two consequative enzymes in purine synthesis. It responds to therapy with uridine, which bypasses the block. 38

Original page 39

4. Lesch Nyhan syndrome: It may responds to adenine. 5.Thiamine-responsive megaloblastic anaemia (DIDMOD syndrome):Diabetes insipidus, diabetes mellitus, optic atrophy and deafness 6.Megaloblastic refractory anemia: AML (M6), MDS and sideroblastic anemia 7.Acute Megaloblastic Anemia (Nitric oxide intoxication): oxidation of Cob I to Cob II → inactivation of methylcobalamin and methionine synthetase  acute megaloblastic anemia  rapid reduction of total leucocytic count and platelets. Methyl malonic aciduria doesn’t occur at first but after generalized depletion of Cob leading to methyl malonic aciduria in serum, urine and Cerebro-spinal fluid.

Pathogenesis

1-Folate or vitamin B12 deficiency → ↓conversion of dUMP into dTMP → ↓DNA synthesis and cell division → ↓ number of cells especially the rapidly dividing cells and nucleo- cytoplasmoic asynchrony. 2-Folate or vitamin B12 deficiency → ↓ the S-adenosyle methionine (SAM) → ↓methyation of lipids, myelin, basic protein, DOPA and DNA with high homocysteine level and increase S- adenosyl homocysteine (SAH) with reduced SAM/SAH ratio that predispose to malignancy

Clinical picture of megaloblastic anemia

1.Bone marrow: Symptoms of pancytopenia including weakness, fatigue, repeated infection and hemorrhagic tendency. 2.Epithelial cell surfaces of mouth, stomach, small intestine and respiratory, urinary and female genital tracts: macrocytosis with increased multinucleate and dying cells. 3.Pregnancy: Sterility, prematurity, open neural tube defect and recurrent fetal loss. 4.Cardiovascular disease: High levels of homocysteine induces thrombosis of coronary, peripheral, pulmonary and cerebrovascular vessels in young age due to:

•Oxidant damage through generation of peroxides.

•Interaction between the free reduced homocysteine and the cysteine residues on 39

coagulation factors, platelets and adhesion molecules or endothelial cells.

•Vascular wall inflammation through the generation of proinflammatory cytokines and interference with key methylation reactions leading to ↑ TF, ↓ thrombomodulin, ↓PS and ↓fibrinolysis. 5.Neurological manifestation (in vitamin B12 deficiency only): Peripheral neuropathy, degeneration of the posterior and pyramidal tracts of the spinal cord, optic atrophy, dementia, visual impairment and impaired mental development in infants. 6.Psychiatric disturbances (in both folate and cobalamin deficiency). 7.Malignancy: Due to ↓ SAM/SAH ratio leading to DNA hypomethylation and due to uracil misincorporation into DNA leading to douple-strand breaks. 8.Other tissues: Folate deficiency decreases the regeneration of cirrhotic liver.

Pernicious Anemia:

Definition: Megaloblastic anemia due to severe lack of intrinsic factor and gastric atrophy.

Pathogenesis:

A. Autoimmune disease caused by antibodies to gastric antigens:

1. Intrinsic factor antibodies (IgG): in the gastric juice of 80% of patients:

•Blocking or type I antibodies (55%): Inhibit the binding of the intrinsic factor to Cobalamin. They are also found in: thyrotoxicosis, myxedema, Hashimoto’s disease, diabetes mellitus and relatives of pernicious anemia patients.

•Binding, type II or precipitating antibodies (35%): inhibit the attachment of the intrinsic factor to the ileal mucosa. It crosses the placenta. 3.Parietal cell antibodies: (in serum of 90% of patients). They are also found in relatives of PA patients, simple atrophic gastritis, chronic active hepatitis, thyroid disorders, addison’s disease and rheumatoid arthritis. 4.Gastrin receptor antibodies 40

Original page 41

B. Association with other autoimmune diseases:

1-Type I intrinsic factor antibodies: found in thyrotoxicosis, myxedema, Hashimoto’s disease, diabetes mellitus and relatives of pernicious anemia patients. 2-Type II intrinsic factor antibodies  not associated with other diseases. 3. Antiparietal cell antibodies: found in relatives of PA patients, simple atrophic gastritis, chronic active hepatitis, thyroid disorders, addison’s disease and rheumatoid arthritis. A.Response to steroids: at least temporarily, with relapse when withdrawn. B.Hypogammaglobulinemia with absent plasma cells in the gastric lesions.

Laboratory findings

1.CBC: Pancytopenia with MCV,  MCH and Normal MCHC. MCV > 100 FL except if associated with iron deficiency, thalassemia trait or excess RBCs fragmentation. 2.Blood film: Oval macrocytes which are fully hemoglobinized, anisocytosis, poikylocytosis, ovalocytes, elliptocytes, excess fragmentation in severe cases, basophilic stippling, Howell jolly bodies and Cabot ring (Cytoplasmic spindle), hypersegmented neutrophils which is an early sign and disappears two weeks after treatment due to the short life span of neutrophils and giant metamyelocytes which persist after treatment Occasionally, there may be leucoerythroblastic blood picture is seen. 3.Reticulocytes: Less than expected for the degree of anemia due to decreased cellular division and the ineffective erythropoiesis 4.Bone marrow: A-Hypercellular with normal or decreased M:E ratio. Absolute myeloid count increases but M/E ratio decreases due to more increase of erythroid precursors. B-The bone marrow is megaloblastic:

○Erythroid megaloblastic changes: Nucleo-cytoplasmic asynchrony with open fine lacy stippled chromatin and normal cytoplasmic maturation and hemoglobinization, increased mitosis and dying cells, multinuclearity, fragmented nucleus (Karyorhexis) and predominance of early precursors due to selective death of mature cells. 41

○Granlopoiesis megaloblastic changes: Hypersegmented neutrophils and abnormal giant forms of metamyelocytes and bands which persist after treatment.

○Megakaryocytic megaloblastic changes: Large hyperpolypoid megakaryocytes. C-Iron stain: Increased iron in both macrophages and normoblasts, increases sideroblasts and increased siderotic granules which are randomly distributed. 4-Ineffective erythropoiesis: Reticulocytes less than expected from the degree of anemia, erythroid hyperplasia,  Serum lysozyme, ↑ Indirect bilirubin, urobilinogen and stercobilinogen,  haptoglobin,  LDH to 1000-10.000 IU/dl with LDH1is more than LDH2,  Serum iron with  plasma iron clearance,  serum Ferritin,  red cell utilization, positive urine hemosiderin and  Carbon monoxide production. 5-Chromosomes: Rapidly proliferating cells show random breaks, reduced contraction, spreading of the centromere, and the exaggeration of secondary chromosomal constrictions and overprominent satellites. 6-Investigation of B12 and folate deficiency: A-Therapeutic trial: Intramuscular Cobalamin injection and oral 100-200g folate daily: th Reticulocytes increase after 3 days and reaches a peak on the 7 day, BM returns normoblastic in days, neutrophils and platelets counts return normal in 7 days.CNS symptoms is relieved in 6 months and anemic symptoms are relieved. Monitoring by methyle-molonic acid and homocysteine is better than monitoring vitamin B12 level because they decrease only with effective treatment. B-Serum vitamin B12 level:sensitive but not specific (40-50% specificity) by radio- immunoassays - ELISA - Chemiluminescence. C-Serum holo-TCII:better than serum vitamin B12 measurement. D-Measurement of Serum folate using ELISA, radioimmunassays or microbiological assays: Low level in folate deficiency and high level in Cobalamin deficiency. E-Measurement of red cell folate: Low in both Cobamin and folate deficiency. 42

F-Deoxyuridine suppression test: The conversion of dUMP to dTMP decreases with no inhibition of thymidine kinase leading to increased uptake of radioactive thymidine. G-High levels of serum and urine methyle-malonic acid: increase in Cobalamin or folate deficiency before hematological abnormalities or subnormal Cobalamin levels and decrease only with effective treatment. H-High levels of serum homocysteine: not widely used for diagnosis of Cobalamin or folate deficiency but usually used in thrombophilia screening I-Schilling test: Less frequently used due to hazards of radioisotopes Overnight fasting ↓ Intramuscular injection of 1 mg of hydroxycobalamin ↓ Oral intake of 1ug of radioactive Cobalamin ↓ Measurement of the radioactivity in 24 hour urine 10% of the oral intake or more Less than 10% of the oral intake  Normal absorption Give oral intrinsic factor with the oral radioactive Cobalamin  Measurement of the radioactivity in 24 hour urine 10% of the oral intake or more Less than 10% of the oral intake  Pernicious anemia or other causes of intrinsic factor deficiency oral antibiotic for one week  Measurement of the radioactivity in 24 hour urine 10% of the oral intake or more Less than 10% of the oral intake  Blind loop syndrome or other causes of intestinal colonization Ileal disease 43

J-Investigation of pernicious anemia:

I- Gastric secretion studies (rarely performed): C.Intrinsic factor: measured by its Cobalamin binding after maximum stimulation by gastrin < 250 unit/h D.HCl : Resting juice pH is more than7, and maximum stimulation with pentagastrin decreases pH by 1 or less with Histamin fast achlorhydria (No increases in gastric HCl after histamine stimulation). II. Gastric biopsy

–Atrophy of all layers of body and fundus with preservation of the antrum

–Loss of glandular elements: Absence of parietal and chief cells with replacement of them by mucous cells

–Mixed inflammatory cell infiltrate (plasma cells and lymphocytes with excess CD4 cells) and perhaps intestinal metaplasia.

–Helicobacter pylori infection: positive in early stages and then replaced by an immune process.

III. Specific antibodies in serum:

–Intrinsic factor antibodies.

–Parietal cell antibodies. IV. Serum gastrin level: 200 g/L or more V. Serum pepsinogen I levels: less 30 g/L with low pepsinogen I/ pepsinogen II ratio.

Management of megaloblastic anaemia:

a)Treatment of cobalamin deficiency: Correction of the underlying cause and Intramuscular hydroxocobalamin injection. b)Treatment of folate deficiency:Therapeutic folate (oral or parenteral)

–Before large doses of folic acid are given, cobalamin deficiency must be excluded and corrected, otherwise cobalamin neuropathy may develop. c)Severe megaloblastic anemia: Hospitalization and Transfusion 44

1.Extravasular hemolysis:

A.Corpuscular causes:

a)Membrane disorders:

Anemia of Alcoholism

Definition: It is a form of anemia seen with chronic alcohol intake Pathogenesis:

▪Anemia of chronic disorders: See before.

▪Megaloblastic anemia: due to vitamin B12 and folate deficiency caused by decreased intake due to anorexia, decreased absorption and decreased folate dependent enzymes

▪Iron deficiency anemia due to decreased intake, decreased absorption and chronic blood loss

▪Sidroblastic anemia due to mitochondrial toxicity

▪Splenomegaly which causes dilution and may be complicated by Hypersplenism

▪Toxic suppression of the bone marrow

▪Hemolytic anemia due to lipoprotein abnormalities and severe hypophosphatemia

Anemia of Protein Malnutrition:

1-Decreased globin 2-Decreased erythropoietin 3- Associated with folate and iron deficiency

○Priority is to hemoglobin synthesis before plasma protein or tissue protein synthesis. So, protein deficiency alone rarely cause normocytic normochromic anemia.

Anemia of Scurvy:

○Normocytic normochromic anemia and may be microcytic hypochromic anemia due to decreased iron absorption

○Commonly associated folate deficiency 121
